hypotheses.title: LSASS Handle with Credential-Access Memory Mask
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor with elevated access on Windows is suspected of reading lsass.exe process memory to extract authentication material. Hunt for non-system processes opening handles to lsass.exe with credential-access or all-access masks, particularly when CallTrace includes UNKNOWN or unexpected DLLs indicating direct syscall or manual API use.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 10
pivots.detail: TargetImage = lsass.exe AND GrantedAccess IN (0x1010, 0x1038, 0x1400, 0x1410, 0x1438, 0x143a, 0x1fffff, 0x1f0fff) AND SourceImage NOT IN (WerFault.exe, WerFaultSecure.exe, Sysmon64.exe, MsMpEng.exe, csrss.exe)

pivots.label: CallTrace anomaly
pivots.detail: CallTrace containing UNKNOWN = direct syscall (NanoDump, custom loaders). CallTrace ending in dbgcore.dll or dbghelp.dll = debugging API path used by ProcDump and older Mimikatz. Modern Mimikatz routes through ntdll.dll alone.

pivots.label: Timing & frequency
pivots.detail: LSASS access >30 min after the last user logon, from a process with no prior LSASS access history, or clustered with 5+ unique source processes within 10 minutes — all significantly raise confidence.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=10 TargetImage=*lsass* GrantedAccess IN (0x1010,0x1038,0x1400,0x1410,0x1fffff) SourceImage NOT IN (WerFault.exe,Sysmon64.exe,MsMpEng.exe)

mitigations.name: Credential Access Protection
mitigations.detail: Enable Windows Credential Guard to move LSASS secrets into VSM — even with a valid handle, credential material is inaccessible.

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Enable LSASS RunAsPPL (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\RunAsPPL=1) and Sysmon process access auditing to catch credential-access handle attempts in real time.

hypotheses.fpr: AV/EDR products, WerFault.exe, Sysmon itself, and tools such as Process Explorer all legitimately access LSASS. Exclude by signed binary + known install path. Alert only when SourceImage is not in an org-maintained allowlist.

hypotheses.title: comsvcs.dll MiniDump Abuse via rundll32
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of abusing the comsvcs.dll MiniDumpW export via rundll32.exe to dump LSASS memory without deploying external tools. Hunt for rundll32.exe command lines combining comsvcs with MiniDump or ordinal references alongside a PID or the string lsass.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1
pivots.detail: Image = rundll32.exe AND CommandLine contains (comsvcs.dll OR comsvcs) AND CommandLine contains (MiniDump OR #24 OR #65560 OR full)

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 10
pivots.detail: TargetImage = lsass.exe AND CallTrace contains comsvcs.dll AND GrantedAccess = 0x1fffff. Correlate with an EID 1 for rundll32 within 2 seconds of the access event.

pivots.label: PowerShell variant
pivots.detail: Also hunt EID 4104 ScriptBlockText contains 'MiniDump' AND 'comsvcs'.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=1 Image=*rundll32.exe CommandLine=*comsvcs* CommandLine=*(MiniDump|#24|#65560)*

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Block rundll32.exe from invoking comsvcs.dll MiniDumpW via WDAC or AppLocker. Enable LSASS RunAsPPL to prevent the dump from completing.

mitigations.name: Credential Access Protection
mitigations.detail: Enable Credential Guard to render the resulting dump file useless for credential extraction — LSASS secrets remain protected in VSM.

hypotheses.fpr: No legitimate administrative use case invokes comsvcs.dll MiniDump against lsass.exe. Near-zero FPR. Confirm by checking for output .dmp file creation within seconds of the rundll32 event.

hypotheses.title: SysInternals ProcDump Targeting LSASS
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using SysInternals ProcDump to write a full LSASS memory dump to disk for offline credential extraction. Hunt for procdump.exe or procdump64.exe process creation with command-line arguments naming lsass by name or PID, especially when executed from non-standard paths or unusual parent processes.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1
pivots.detail: Image endswith (procdump.exe OR procdump64.exe) AND (CommandLine contains '-ma lsass' OR CommandLine contains '-mm lsass' OR CommandLine contains lsass.exe)

pivots.label: Parent process
pivots.detail: ProcDump launched from cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wmiexec, or psexec parent is highly suspicious. Execution from a UNC path indicates remote tool staging.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 11
pivots.detail: File created by procdump.exe with .dmp extension in a temp or user-writable directory within seconds of process creation confirms a successful dump.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=1 Image=*(procdump|procdump64).exe CommandLine=*lsass*

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Block procdump.exe from targeting lsass.exe via AppLocker publisher rules. Enable LSASS RunAsPPL so ProcDump receives access denied.

mitigations.name: Credential Access Protection
mitigations.detail: Enable Credential Guard — even with a dump file, Credential Guard-protected secrets appear as encrypted blobs that cannot be decrypted offline.

hypotheses.fpr: ProcDump is a legitimate SysInternals tool. Allowlist execution from C:\Program Files when the target is not lsass and the parent is a recognized IDE or support session. Alert on: lsass target, unusual parent, staging path, off-hours.

hypotheses.title: LSASS Dump File Creation in Staging Path
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of having successfully dumped LSASS memory to a file in a staging path for subsequent exfiltration. Hunt for .dmp files created in world-writable or temp directories by any process with prior LSASS handle activity, or by Task Manager as a low-tech operator dump technique.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 11
pivots.detail: TargetFilename endswith .dmp AND (TargetFilename contains lsass OR Image endswith taskmgr.exe OR Image endswith procdump.exe OR Image endswith rundll32.exe) AND path matches (%TEMP%\* OR C:\Windows\Temp\* OR C:\ProgramData\*)

pivots.label: File size heuristic
pivots.detail: LSASS memory dumps are typically 30–150 MB. A large .dmp file in %TEMP% or AppData created outside a crash scenario is a strong indicator — correlate file size with creation process.

pivots.label: Task Manager variant
pivots.detail: Image = taskmgr.exe AND TargetFilename contains lsass AND TargetFilename endswith .dmp — covers the low-tech manual dump technique documented in PYSA/Mespinoza campaigns.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=11 TargetFilename=*lsass*.dmp TargetFilename path IN (%TEMP%,C:\Windows\Temp,C:\ProgramData) Image NOT IN (WerFault.exe)

mitigations.name: Credential Access Protection
mitigations.detail: Enable Credential Guard — a dump file containing VSM-protected material yields no usable credentials without the VSM key.

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Configure EDR file-creation rules alerting on large .dmp files in temp paths by non-WerFault processes; pair with LSASS handle auditing to correlate the full chain.

refs.label: DFIR Report — PYSA Task Manager dumps

hypotheses.fpr: WerFault.exe and WerFaultSecure.exe legitimately create LSASS-related crash dumps — exclude those processes. Developer crash dump sessions may produce .dmp files in custom paths; correlate with active debugging sessions.

hypotheses.title: BYOVD / PPL Bypass Driver Load Before LSASS Access
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of loading a vulnerable or unsigned kernel driver (BYOVD) to strip PPL protection from lsass.exe before performing a memory dump. Hunt for unsigned driver loads from staging paths within 60 seconds of a process accessing LSASS memory — the driver load is the pre-condition that makes the dump possible.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 6 → EID 10 chain
pivots.detail: EID 6: ImageLoaded in (%TEMP%\* OR C:\ProgramData\* OR C:\Windows\Temp\*) AND Signed=false OR SignatureStatus=Untrusted, followed within 60s by EID 10 TargetImage=lsass.exe from same or child process.

pivots.label: Known BYOVD driver hashes
pivots.detail: Correlate EID 6 ImageLoaded hashes against known vulnerable drivers: DBUtil_2_3.sys (CVE-2021-21551), gdrv.sys, RTCore64.sys, AMSDK.sys, procexp152.sys. Block via WDAC vulnerable driver blocklist.

pivots.label: PPL stripping via handle manipulation
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 10: TargetImage=lsass.exe AND GrantedAccess=0x1fffff from a process that was not able to access LSASS before driver load. Pair with WMI or kernel object manager access events if available.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=6 Signed=false | join EventCode=10 TargetImage=*lsass* [by host] | where timediff < 60s

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Deploy Microsoft WDAC Vulnerable Driver Blocklist policy. Enable Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI) to prevent unsigned kernel drivers from loading.

mitigations.name: Credential Access Protection
mitigations.detail: Enable Windows Credential Guard — even if LSASS PPL is bypassed, Credential Guard isolates secrets in VSM so they are unreachable via memory reads.

refs.label: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities — BYOVD drivers

hypotheses.fpr: Near-zero FPR when chaining unsigned driver load + LSASS access within 60 seconds. Signed but revoked drivers (common in BYOVD) may not trigger Signed=false — add revocation status check. Legitimate kernel debugger sessions (WinDbg, kd.exe) may load unsigned drivers; exclude known development environments.

hypotheses.title: Silent Process Exit / WER Registry Hijack for Auto LSASS Dump
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of configuring the Silent Process Exit or Windows Error Reporting (WER) registry mechanism to automatically trigger a memory dump of lsass.exe without running an external dumper. Hunt for registry writes to the SilentProcessExit or WER LocalDumps keys targeting lsass.exe, followed by WerFault.exe spawned with LSASS as the monitored process.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 — Registry set
pivots.detail: TargetObject contains HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit\lsass.exe AND EventType=SetValue. Fields: GlobalFlag, ReportingMode, MonitorProcess. Written by any non-SYSTEM process is suspicious.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 — WER LocalDumps
pivots.detail: TargetObject matches HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps\lsass.exe\DumpType = 2 (full dump). Followed by WerFault.exe EID 1 with CommandLine containing -p [lsass pid].

pivots.label: WerFault dump file creation
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 11: WerFault.exe creating .dmp file in C:\Windows\Temp\ or %LOCALAPPDATA%\CrashDumps\ with large file size (30–150 MB) at an unexpected time — no user-facing crash dialog preceding it.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=13 TargetObject=*SilentProcessExit*lsass* | alert critical

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Monitor and restrict writes to HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit via registry auditing and EDR rules.

mitigations.name: Operating System Configuration
mitigations.detail: Enable RunAsPPL for LSASS (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\RunAsPPL=1) so WerFault cannot dump it without PPL-level trust.

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate crash reporting infrastructure may write to WER LocalDumps paths during genuine application crashes. The key differentiator is the target process (lsass.exe), the registry write originating from a non-SYSTEM, non-WerFault process, and off-hours timing.

hypotheses.title: Sqldumper.exe LOLBin Abused to Dump LSASS
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of abusing sqldumper.exe, a signed Microsoft SQL Server utility, to create a full memory dump of lsass.exe without deploying unsigned tools. Hunt for sqldumper.exe executed outside a SQL Server process tree, with command-line arguments targeting a PID associated with lsass.exe, and output path in a staging directory.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — sqldumper invocation
pivots.detail: Image endswith sqldumper.exe AND ParentImage NOT IN (sqlservr.exe, sqlagent.exe, sqlbrowser.exe) AND CommandLine matches pattern: sqldumper.exe [PID] 0 0x01100 [output_path]. PID will be the lsass.exe PID at the time.

pivots.label: Output file creation
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 11: sqldumper.exe creates SQLDmpr*.mdmp in %TEMP%, C:\ProgramData\, or other staging path within seconds of process creation. File size >30 MB indicates full process dump.

pivots.label: Correlation with lsass PID
pivots.detail: Cross-correlate the PID in sqldumper CommandLine with running processes. If PID resolves to lsass.exe at event time, confidence is critical. Use Sysmon EID 5 (process terminate) and EID 1 timestamps to build process lifetime map.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=1 Image=*sqldumper.exe NOT (ParentImage=*sqlservr*) | alert

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Block sqldumper.exe execution via WDAC or AppLocker on non-SQL-Server systems. Alert on any sqldumper.exe execution outside SQL Server install directory.

mitigations.name: Credential Access Protection
mitigations.detail: Enable Credential Guard to prevent credential extraction from LSASS even if a dump is obtained.

hypotheses.fpr: Sqldumper.exe is legitimate when spawned by SQL Server processes (sqlservr.exe, sqlagent.exe). Alert exclusively when the parent is cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe, or any non-SQL-Server binary, and the output path is outside the SQL diagnostic directory.

hypotheses.title: Direct Syscall / Fork-Clone LSASS Dump (NanoDump Fingerprint)
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using a custom tool that bypasses user-mode API hooks via direct syscalls or clones the LSASS process before dumping, leaving a CallTrace anomaly as the primary forensic signal. Hunt for LSASS access events where CallTrace contains UNKNOWN memory regions or does not terminate in ntdll.dll, indicating a direct syscall path that bypasses EDR hook points.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 10 — UNKNOWN CallTrace
pivots.detail: TargetImage=lsass.exe AND CallTrace contains UNKNOWN. The UNKNOWN segment indicates code executing from unbacked memory — characteristic of direct syscall stubs, reflective loaders, or shellcode. High confidence when GrantedAccess = 0x1fffff.

pivots.label: NanoDump fork-clone artifact
pivots.detail: NanoDump forks LSASS (clones the process) then dumps the clone. Look for: a short-lived process with the same image path as lsass.exe OR a process with ParentPID=lsass.exe PID appearing briefly. Sysmon EID 1+5 pair on lsass-like process within 5 seconds.

pivots.label: Encrypted/compressed output file
pivots.detail: NanoDump writes an XOR-encrypted or compressed dump (not a standard .dmp) to disk. Hunt EID 11: file created by an unusual process in staging path with .dmp, .bin, .tmp extension and file size 30–200 MB within seconds of the EID 10 event.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=10 TargetImage=*lsass* CallTrace=*UNKNOWN* | alert critical

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: EDRs with kernel-level callbacks (minifilter + ETW kernel) can detect direct syscalls that bypass user-mode hooks. Enable kernel telemetry on security products. HVCI prevents most direct-syscall techniques.

mitigations.name: Credential Access Protection
mitigations.detail: Credential Guard isolates LSASS secrets even if memory is successfully dumped — the secrets are in VSM and appear as opaque blobs in the dump.

hypotheses.fpr: UNKNOWN CallTrace segments are rare in legitimate software. Primary false positive source is security software with in-process trampolines or kernel callbacks not registered via standard module loading. Validate by correlating with process reputation, parent, and signed status.

hypotheses.title: Registry Save of SAM / SECURITY / SYSTEM Hives via reg.exe
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using reg.exe to save the SAM, SECURITY, and SYSTEM registry hives to disk for offline password hash extraction. Hunt for reg.exe executing a save or export of any of these three hives — especially when SAM and SYSTEM are both saved in the same session, as both are required to decrypt the password hashes.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — reg.exe hive save
pivots.detail: Image endswith reg.exe AND CommandLine matches (save|export) AND CommandLine contains (HKLM\SAM OR HKLM\SECURITY OR HKLM\SYSTEM OR hklm\sam OR hklm\security OR hklm\system). Alert as critical when SAM and SYSTEM are saved within 60 seconds of each other from the same session.

pivots.label: Output file creation
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 11: file created by reg.exe in %TEMP%, C:\Windows\Temp, C:\ProgramData, or user home directory with extensions .hiv, .save, .bak, .dat, .sam, or no extension. File size typically 10–100 KB for SAM, 10–30 KB for SECURITY.

pivots.label: Privilege requirement
pivots.detail: reg.exe hive save requires SeBackupPrivilege or local administrator. EID 4656: object access audit for HKLM\SAM with AccessMask 0x20019. Correlate with EID 4672 (special privilege logon) to confirm administrator-level execution.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=1 Image=*reg.exe CommandLine=*(save|export)* CommandLine=*(HKLM\SAM|HKLM\SECURITY|HKLM\SYSTEM)*

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.detail: Enforce strong, unique passwords — offline SAM cracking yields NTLM hashes which are trivially cracked for weak passwords via hashcat/john.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict local administrator accounts. Disable built-in Administrator. Require MFA for privileged access to reduce the attack surface for hive extraction.

hypotheses.fpr: IT and backup tools (backup agents, Veeam, Windows Server Backup) legitimately access registry hives via VSS — they do not call reg.exe save. Legitimate reg.exe save operations in enterprise are extremely rare outside controlled migration tasks. Exclude parent processes that are signed backup software. Alert whenever reg.exe saves SAM regardless of parent.

hypotheses.title: SAM / NTDS File Theft via Volume Shadow Copy
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of creating or accessing a VSS shadow copy to retrieve SAM or NTDS credential files without triggering live registry access controls. Hunt for vssadmin or wmic shadow creation followed by file copy operations targeting the config or NTDS directory path from within a shadow volume path.

pivots.label: Shadow creation
pivots.detail: EID 1: vssadmin.exe 'create shadow' OR wmic shadowcopy call create. If these appear on a domain controller, risk is critical. Correlate with subsequent file copy within 5 minutes from same session.

pivots.label: SAM copy from shadow
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 1: cmd.exe OR copy.exe OR xcopy.exe OR robocopy.exe CommandLine matching path \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy*\Windows\System32\config\SAM. Also: esentutl.exe /y targeting shadow path.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 24 — Raw disk read
pivots.detail: RawAccessRead on device path \\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy* by non-backup process. Also EID 11: SAM or ntds.dit file appearing outside its canonical path (C:\Windows\System32\config\ or C:\Windows\NTDS\).

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=1 Image=*vssadmin* CommandLine=*create* | followby EventCode=1 CommandLine=*HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy* within 300s

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Restrict VSS creation and management to backup service accounts. EDR rules alerting on vssadmin.exe by non-backup parent processes.

mitigations.name: Operating System Configuration
mitigations.detail: Configure SACL auditing on NTDS.dit and SAM file paths. Monitor EID 4663 (object access) for SAM/NTDS file reads outside backup windows.

refs.label: CISA AA23-075A — LockBit shadow copy deletion
DFIR Report — Shadow copy credential theft

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate backup solutions (Veeam, Windows Server Backup, Acronis) create VSS shadows routinely. The key differentiator is the SUBSEQUENT file copy targeting SAM, NTDS.dit, or SECURITY hive paths from the shadow volume. Exclude backup service accounts by SID and parent process signature.

hypotheses.title: Remote SAM Extraction via Impacket / CrackMapExec
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor with valid credentials is suspected of remotely extracting SAM hashes from a target host using Impacket secretsdump or CrackMapExec without deploying any binary to the target. Hunt for unexpected network authentication to the target followed by remote registry access over SMB, which is the transport mechanism for remote SAM extraction.

pivots.label: EID 4624 type 3 logon + registry pipe
pivots.detail: On target host: EID 4624 type 3 (network logon) from a workstation or attacker IP, followed within 30 seconds by EID 5145: network share access to \PIPE\winreg (Windows Remote Registry protocol). The combination is the exact fingerprint of secretsdump SAM extraction.

pivots.label: Remote registry service
pivots.detail: EID 7036 (Windows): RemoteRegistry service changed to Running state immediately before the 5145 event. secretsdump enables the service on demand. Alert on RemoteRegistry starting outside maintenance windows, especially on workstations.

pivots.label: Large outbound SMB transfer
pivots.detail: Network: >50 KB data transferred outbound from target on port 445 within 60 seconds of the network logon. The extracted hashes and registry data are returned over the same SMB session.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=5145 ShareName=*PIPE* RelativeTargetName=winreg | join EventCode=4624 LogonType=3 [by host, within 30s]

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Disable Remote Registry service on workstations and member servers. Restrict who can connect to ADMIN$ and IPC$ shares via host-based firewall rules.

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.detail: Enforce unique local administrator passwords via LAPS to prevent lateral movement after initial SAM extraction yields reusable credentials.

hypotheses.fpr: Remote Registry access is used by some RMM tools (ConnectWise, Kaseya) and Group Policy infrastructure. Exclude known RMM source IPs and service accounts. The strongest FPR reduction is alerting only when RemoteRegistry is started dynamically (EID 7036 transition from Stopped to Running).

hypotheses.title: ntdsutil IFM Snapshot for Offline NTDS.dit Extraction
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor with Domain Admin or Backup Operator privileges on a domain controller is suspected of using ntdsutil to create an Install-from-Media snapshot that contains a full copy of the NTDS.dit Active Directory database. Hunt for ntdsutil.exe execution on any host — especially domain controllers — with IFM-related command arguments, as this is almost never a legitimate administrative activity outside planned DC provisioning.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — ntdsutil IFM
pivots.detail: Image endswith ntdsutil.exe AND CommandLine contains (ifm OR 'install from media' OR 'activate instance ntds' OR 'create full'). Any execution outside a documented DC promotion/demotion change window should be treated as critical.

pivots.label: Output directory creation
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 11: ntds.dit file creation in a non-NTDS path (not C:\Windows\NTDS\) by ntdsutil.exe or by a process running as SYSTEM shortly after. Output dir is typically specified by the attacker — check for staging paths.

pivots.label: Privilege audit
pivots.detail: EID 4672 (Special Logon) with SeBackupPrivilege and SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege in the privileges list, immediately before ntdsutil execution. EID 4648 shows the account used. Cross-reference with the account's normal behavior baseline.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=1 Image=*ntdsutil.exe CommandLine=*(ifm|install from media)* | alert critical on DC hosts

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict membership of Backup Operators and Domain Admins. Require privileged access workstations (PAWs) for DC administration. Alert on any non-scheduled ntdsutil execution.

mitigations.name: Operating System Configuration
mitigations.detail: Enable advanced audit policy on domain controllers for DS Access (EID 4662) and Audit Privilege Use. Forward DC logs to SIEM with low-latency alerting.

hypotheses.fpr: ntdsutil IFM is used legitimately only when provisioning a new DC from media. In most enterprises this happens once during initial deployment or controlled DR testing. Allowlist only when change management records confirm a DC promotion activity in the same time window.

hypotheses.title: diskshadow.exe LOLBin Abuse for NTDS.dit Copy
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a domain controller is suspected of abusing diskshadow.exe, a signed Microsoft utility, to create and expose a VSS shadow copy and then extract NTDS.dit without invoking vssadmin directly. Hunt for diskshadow.exe executed with a script file argument, followed by esentutl or copy operations targeting the shadow volume path containing NTDS.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — diskshadow with script
pivots.detail: Image endswith diskshadow.exe AND (CommandLine contains '/s' OR CommandLine contains '-s'). The script file is attacker-controlled and typically contains: set context persistent nowriters / add volume C: / create / expose %f: e: / exec cmd.exe /c copy e:\NTDS\ntds.dit C:\Temp\.

pivots.label: NTDS.dit outside canonical path
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 11: file creation of ntds.dit in any path other than C:\Windows\NTDS\ by any process other than lsass.exe or ntdsutil.exe. This is an almost guaranteed true positive.

pivots.label: esentutl copy chain
pivots.detail: EID 1: esentutl.exe /y [shadow volume path]\ntds.dit /d [staging path]\ntds.dit — the /y flag is the copy flag. Immediately following diskshadow execution confirms the NTDS theft chain.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=1 Image=*diskshadow.exe CommandLine=*(-s|/s)* | followby EventCode=11 TargetFilename=*ntds.dit* within 300s

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Restrict diskshadow.exe via WDAC or AppLocker on domain controllers. Alert on any diskshadow.exe execution as it has no routine interactive administrative use.

mitigations.name: Operating System Configuration
mitigations.detail: Configure SACL on C:\Windows\NTDS\ntds.dit to audit all non-lsass read access. Forward EID 4663 from DCs to SIEM.

hypotheses.fpr: diskshadow.exe in interactive mode (no /s flag) may be used by storage admins. The /s script mode is almost exclusively malicious in post-compromise scenarios. Zero legitimate use case for diskshadow creating a shadow and immediately copying ntds.dit.

hypotheses.title: Remote NTDS Extraction via Impacket secretsdump
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor with Domain Admin credentials is suspected of remotely extracting all Active Directory password hashes from a domain controller using Impacket secretsdump without interacting with the DC file system directly. Hunt for unexpected administrative SMB authentication to a DC followed by VSS shadow creation and large data transfer — the network-only NTDS dump signature.

pivots.label: EID 4624 + VSS service on DC
pivots.detail: On DC: EID 4624 type 3 logon from non-DC, non-admin workstation IP, immediately followed by EID 7036: Volume Shadow Copy service transitioning to Running. secretsdump triggers VSS remotely to access ntds.dit.

pivots.label: ADMIN$ share + large SMB transfer
pivots.detail: EID 5145: ADMIN$ share access from attacker IP on DC, combined with >1 MB outbound SMB data transfer within 60 seconds. The encrypted NTDS hashes are returned over SMB.

pivots.label: EID 4662 — NTDS replication or access
pivots.detail: EID 4662 on DC: accesses to NTDS.dit-related object or DS-Replication attributes by the authenticated account. Correlate with the source IP from the network logon. If the IP is a workstation (not another DC), escalate immediately.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=4624 LogonType=3 TargetHost=*DC* | followby EventCode=7036 ServiceName=VSS State=Running within 60s [on same host]

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Use tiered admin model: Tier-0 accounts (DA/EA) restricted to PAWs. Block Tier-0 accounts from logging into non-DC systems. Require MFA for all DC admin access.

mitigations.name: Active Directory Configuration
mitigations.detail: Restrict who can initiate VSS on DCs. Monitor DC-to-workstation authentication patterns — DCs should rarely initiate or receive logins from regular workstations.

hypotheses.fpr: DC-to-DC replication legitimately triggers VSS and NTDS access. Baseline which IPs are DCs and exclude DC machine accounts. The critical differentiator is a workstation or member server IP — not a DC — initiating the SMB logon followed by VSS.

hypotheses.title: Registry Save of SECURITY Hive for LSA Secret Extraction
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of saving the HKLM\SECURITY registry hive — which contains LSA secrets including service account passwords, DPAPI master keys, and cached domain credentials — for offline extraction. Hunt for reg.exe saving SECURITY combined with SYSTEM in the same session, as the SYSTEM hive contains the boot key required to decrypt LSA secrets.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — SECURITY hive save
pivots.detail: Image endswith reg.exe AND CommandLine matches (save|export) AND CommandLine contains (HKLM\SECURITY OR hklm\security). Escalate to critical when SYSTEM hive is also saved within the same session (60-second window).

pivots.label: SECURITY hive registry access
pivots.detail: EID 4656: handle requested to HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets or subkeys with AccessMask 0x20019 (read) by a process that is not lsass.exe or svchost.exe. Non-system processes accessing LSA secrets subkeys is anomalous.

pivots.label: Post-extraction service logon
pivots.detail: After extraction, watch for EID 4624 logons using service account credentials from unusual source IPs — adversaries use extracted service passwords for lateral movement within minutes of extraction.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=1 Image=*reg.exe CommandLine=*HKLM\\SECURITY* CommandLine=*(save|export)*

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Limit local administrator accounts. Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) to prevent service account password reuse — gMSA passwords are 240-bit random values that cannot be extracted usefully.

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Enable enhanced LSA protection (RunAsPPL) to prevent unauthorized LSA secret access. Audit HKLM\SECURITY key access via Windows auditing policies.

refs.label: CISA AA22-074A — Destructive malware using LSA secrets

hypotheses.fpr: Backup solutions with system-level access legitimately read SECURITY hive data, but not via reg.exe save. Alert on any reg.exe save of HKLM\SECURITY — there is essentially no legitimate interactive administrative use case. Backup agents use VSS or API access, not reg.exe.

hypotheses.title: Mimikatz lsadump::secrets Live LSA Secret Extraction
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor with elevated privileges is suspected of running Mimikatz lsadump::secrets (or equivalent) to extract LSA secrets directly from LSASS memory, immediately pivoting to lateral movement using extracted service account credentials. Hunt for broad LSASS memory access followed within minutes by service account logons from the same host to new targets.

pivots.label: LSASS access with secret-read mask
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 10: TargetImage=lsass.exe AND GrantedAccess IN (0x1410, 0x1010, 0x0010) from a non-system binary. The 0x1410 mask (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ) is the Mimikatz lsadump::secrets access pattern.

pivots.label: Post-extraction service account logon
pivots.detail: Within 10 minutes of LSASS access: EID 4624 type 3 logon using a service account (name ending in svc, _svc, -sa, or matching known service account naming) from the compromised host to a new target — lateral movement using extracted service password.

pivots.label: EID 4611 — Debug privilege assignment
pivots.detail: EID 4611: A trusted logon process has been registered (SeDebugPrivilege assignment). Mimikatz requires SeDebugPrivilege before accessing LSASS. This event fires when a process enables debug privilege — correlate with the lsass.exe access event.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=10 TargetImage=*lsass* GrantedAccess=0x1410 | followby EventCode=4624 LogonType=3 [by host] within 600s

mitigations.name: Credential Access Protection
mitigations.detail: Replace service account passwords with Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA). Enable Credential Guard to move LSASS secrets into VSM.

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: EDR with LSASS protection rules. Enable RunAsPPL for LSASS (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\RunAsPPL=1).

refs.label: CISA AA22-074A — FIN7 LSA credential theft

hypotheses.fpr: SeDebugPrivilege assignment (EID 4611) occurs for some legitimate monitoring agents. Focus on pairing EID 4611 with the LSASS access event from the same process. Service account logons for lateral movement will typically target servers the account has no historical logon to — check logon history baseline.

hypotheses.title: Cached Domain Credential Hash Extraction via SECURITY + SYSTEM Hive Pair
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a domain-joined Windows host is suspected of exfiltrating cached domain logon hashes (MSCacheV2 / DCC2) by saving the SECURITY hive (which contains the hashes) and the SYSTEM hive (which contains the boot key needed to decrypt them) for offline hashcat cracking. Hunt for both hives saved within the same session — together they are sufficient to crack cached domain credentials offline.

pivots.label: Dual hive save pattern
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 1: two reg.exe save commands within 60 seconds — one targeting HKLM\SECURITY and one targeting HKLM\SYSTEM — from the same parent process or interactive session. This combination is the exact prerequisite for offline MSCacheV2 cracking with hashcat -m 2100.

pivots.label: Post-cracking logon from attacker
pivots.detail: After exfiltration, watch for domain account logons (EID 4624) from new/unusual source IPs using accounts that last authenticated from the compromised endpoint — indicating successful cracking of cached hashes and use as valid credentials.

pivots.label: Offline staging before exfil
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 11: .hiv, .save, .bak, or similarly named files in %TEMP% or %ProgramData% shortly after the reg.exe events. Often compressed into .zip or .7z immediately before transfer — monitor for archive creation by cmd.exe or powershell.exe in same timeframe.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=1 Image=*reg.exe CommandLine=*HKLM\\SECURITY* | followby Image=*reg.exe CommandLine=*HKLM\\SYSTEM* within 60s

mitigations.name: Credential Access Protection
mitigations.detail: Reduce cached logon count to 0 via GPO (Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache = 0) on servers and privileged systems where offline access is not needed.

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.detail: Long, complex domain passwords significantly increase the time to crack MSCacheV2 hashes. Enforce 20+ character passphrases for privileged accounts — even with GPU cracking rigs, DCC2 with strong passwords is infeasible in reasonable time.

refs.label: CISA AA21-265A — Conti cached credential abuse

hypotheses.fpr: Both SECURITY and SYSTEM hives are accessed by backup tools, but not via reg.exe save. Legitimate GPO-driven registry operations do not use reg.exe save. If reg.exe save of SECURITY is detected, it warrants investigation regardless of context.

hypotheses.title: Mimikatz lsadump::cache Targeted at Cached Privileged Account Hashes
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a domain-joined endpoint is suspected of using Mimikatz lsadump::cache to extract cached domain credential hashes through LSASS, targeting high-value accounts (Domain Admins, service accounts) that have previously logged into the machine. Hunt for LSASS memory access with the Mimikatz credential-access mask, followed by lateral movement attempts using domain administrator credentials from the compromised endpoint.

pivots.label: LSASS access + cached creds context
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 10: TargetImage=lsass.exe from a non-system process. Correlate with: the endpoint's last interactive logon history (EID 4624/4634) to identify which domain accounts have cached credentials on this machine — these are the attacker's targets.

pivots.label: DA account used from workstation
pivots.detail: EID 4624 type 3 from the compromised workstation using a Domain Admin or privileged account, within 30 minutes of the LSASS access event. Domain Admin accounts should never authenticate FROM workstations in a properly segmented environment.

pivots.label: EID 4776 — NTLM auth failure spike
pivots.detail: Multiple EID 4776 NTLM authentication failures from the compromised host in the minutes after LSASS access may indicate the attacker is testing cracked cached hashes against network resources before they are fully cracked.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=4624 LogonType=3 SubjectUserName=*admin* | where source_host is workstation NOT DC | correlate with prior EID=10 TargetImage=lsass

mitigations.name: Credential Access Protection
mitigations.detail: Set CachedLogonsCount to 0 or 1 on servers and privileged-access workstations. This eliminates the attack surface for cached credential extraction on those machines.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Enforce tiered administration — Tier-0 accounts (DA) must never interactively log into Tier-1/2 machines. This prevents privileged caches from appearing on workstations.

refs.label: Red Canary TDR — Credential Access patterns

hypotheses.fpr: LSASS access alone is insufficient — the correlation with privileged account lateral movement is the key signal. Focus detection on the post-extraction behavior (DA logon from workstation) rather than the extraction event alone, which reduces alert fatigue from EDR LSASS access noise.

hypotheses.title: DCSync via DS-Replication Rights Abuse (Primary Detection)
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor with an account granted DS-Replication-Get-Changes and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All rights is suspected of using the DCSync technique to pull all Active Directory password hashes, including krbtgt, without touching the domain controller file system. Hunt for directory replication access events (EID 4662) from accounts that are not domain controller machine accounts and not on the legitimate replication IP baseline.

pivots.label: EID 4662 — Non-DC replication access
pivots.detail: On DC: EID 4662 with Properties containing {19195a5b-6da0-11d0-afd3-00c04fd930c9} (DS-Replication-Get-Changes) AND {1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2} (DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All) AND SubjectUserName does NOT end in $ (machine account) and is not in the known DC list. This is the highest-confidence DCSync signal.

pivots.label: EID 4929 — Replication source removal
pivots.detail: EID 4929: An Active Directory replica source naming context was removed. This fires during DCSync and is a secondary confirmation signal. Combined with EID 4662, confidence approaches 100%.

pivots.label: MSRPC DRS traffic from non-DC
pivots.detail: Network: MS-DRSR (DRS protocol) traffic on dynamic RPC port (49152-65535) from a non-DC source IP to DC. NDR payload containing DRSGetNCChanges RPC operation. Zeek or Suricata with MS-RPC dissection can detect this without Windows event logs.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=4662 Properties=*19195a5b* Properties=*1131f6ad* SubjectUserName!=*$ | alert critical

mitigations.name: Active Directory Configuration
mitigations.detail: Audit and restrict DS-Replication rights. Only DC machine accounts should have DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All. Use BloodHound or PingCastle to enumerate accounts with DCSync rights and remove unauthorized grants.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Enforce least privilege on AD ACLs. Use Protected Users security group for privileged accounts to prevent NTLM use even if hashes are stolen.

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate DC-to-DC replication generates identical EID 4662 events — filter by SubjectUserName ending in $ (machine accounts) and source IPs matching your known DC list. The SubjectUserName NOT ending in $ with replication GUIDs is the definitive true positive condition.

hypotheses.title: DCSync Privilege Pre-Grant via AD ACL Modification
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor with WriteDACL or GenericAll rights on the domain object is suspected of granting a controlled account DCSync replication rights before executing DCSync, enabling persistence and delayed credential harvest. Hunt for modifications to the domain root object's security descriptor that add DS-Replication rights to non-DC accounts — this is the setup phase that precedes DCSync execution.

pivots.label: EID 5136 — Domain object SecurityDescriptor modified
pivots.detail: EID 5136: Directory service object modified where ObjectDN matches the domain root (DC=domain,DC=com) AND AttributeLDAPDisplayName=nTSecurityDescriptor. Any modification to the domain root security descriptor should be investigated — DCSync right grants will appear as ACE additions.

pivots.label: EID 4662 — Permission change audit
pivots.detail: EID 4662 with AccessMask 0x40000 (WriteDACL) or 0x10000000 (GenericAll) on the domain root object. Combined with EID 5136, this shows who made the change.

pivots.label: BloodHound / AD enumeration precursor
pivots.detail: LDAP queries enumerating domain ACLs (ObjectClass=domain, nTSecurityDescriptor attribute reads) from a workstation via LDAP port 389/636 in the hours or days before the ACL modification. BloodHound collectors generate characteristic LDAP query patterns.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=5136 ObjectDN=*DC=* AttributeLDAPDisplayName=nTSecurityDescriptor | alert and investigate

mitigations.name: Active Directory Configuration
mitigations.detail: Regularly audit domain root ACLs with PowerView Get-DomainObjectAcl or BloodHound. Enable EID 5136 auditing on all DCs. Remove unnecessary WriteDACL grants from non-admin accounts.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict WriteDACL on domain objects to the built-in Administrators group and SYSTEM. Monitor AD delegation changes with tools like PingCastle or Purple Knight.

refs.label: CISA AA22-276A — ACL abuse in APT29 operations

hypotheses.fpr: EID 5136 domain object modifications are noisy in environments with active AD management. Focus specifically on nTSecurityDescriptor attribute changes on the domain root object. Changes during off-hours or by accounts not in the AD Admins team are red flags.

hypotheses.title: DCSync Network Fingerprint — DRSGetNCChanges from Workstation
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor is suspected of executing DCSync entirely over the network using Impacket or similar tooling, without placing any binary on disk on the domain controller. Hunt for the MS-DRSR DRSGetNCChanges RPC call originating from a non-DC host — this network-level signature is detectable via IDS/NDR even without Windows event log access to the DC.

pivots.label: MS-DRSR RPC from non-DC IP
pivots.detail: Network IDS/NDR: MSRPC bind to MS-DRSR interface UUID {e3514235-4b06-11d1-ab04-00c04fc2dcd2} from source IP NOT in the known DC IP list. The DRSGetNCChanges opnum 3 call carries the actual hash replication. Zeek: msrpc.log endpoint=DRSR from workstation IP.

pivots.label: Impacket tool fingerprint
pivots.detail: Impacket's MS-RPC implementation has characteristic patterns: specific SMB negotiate dialect order, NTLM authentication with specific field ordering, and RPC bind request with specific AlterContext flags. Network sandbox or protocol analysis can fingerprint Impacket vs. native MS clients.

pivots.label: Large encrypted RPC response
pivots.detail: DRSGetNCChanges returns encrypted NTDS hash data — a large (>100 KB) RPC response from DC to the requesting non-DC host within seconds of the DRS bind is the data exfiltration event. Correlate with EID 4624 type 3 on the DC from the same source IP.

detection_logic.query_hint: zeek msrpc_log endpoint=MS-DRSR src_ip NOT IN dc_ip_list | alert critical

mitigations.name: Active Directory Configuration
mitigations.detail: Implement network segmentation blocking DRS RPC traffic from workstations to DCs. Only DC-to-DC replication should traverse the MSRPC dynamic port range on the DC network segment.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Enforce Protected Users security group membership for DA accounts to block NTLM and force Kerberos only — Impacket's default DCSync path is NTLM which is blocked for Protected Users.

refs.label: CISA AA20-296A — APT29 credential theft tradecraft

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate DC replication uses the same protocol — differentiate solely by source IP. Maintain a precise and current DC IP inventory list. Any DRS traffic from a non-DC IP is a true positive with high confidence.

hypotheses.title: /proc/[pid]/mem Read for In-Memory Credential Extraction on Linux
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Linux host is suspected of reading /proc/[pid]/mem of a credential-holding process (sshd, sudo, PAM, gnome-keyring) to extract cleartext passwords or session tokens from process memory. Hunt for non-root processes or unexpected binaries opening the /proc/[pid]/mem path of authentication daemons, as tools like LaZagne and Mimipenguin use this technique for agentless credential theft.

pivots.label: Auditd — /proc/*/mem openat
pivots.detail: Auditd rule: -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S openat,open -F path=/proc -F key=proc_mem_access. Alert on: auid!=0 (non-root) accessing /proc/[sshd_pid]/mem OR any process accessing /proc/[pid]/mem where the target pid belongs to sshd, sudo, or gnome-keyring-daemon.

pivots.label: ptrace against authentication daemons
pivots.detail: Auditd: syscall=ptrace AND a0=PTRACE_ATTACH (0x10) targeting sshd, sudo, or PAM-using processes. ptrace is the traditional method before /proc/mem became accessible. Also: /proc/[pid]/syscall reads indicating syscall interception.

pivots.label: LaZagne / Mimipenguin execution
pivots.detail: Process creation: execve of python3 / lazagne.py OR mimipenguin.sh OR similar script. LaZagne on Linux reads /proc/*/mem for Firefox, Chrome, OpenSSH, and gnome-keyring. File creation: output file in /tmp or /dev/shm by an unusual parent process.

detection_logic.query_hint: auditd type=SYSCALL syscall=openat a2=*mem* key=proc_mem_access uid!=0 | alert

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Enable Linux kernel lockdown mode (lockdown=confidentiality) and restrict ptrace scope via /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope=2 (only admin ptrace). These significantly limit /proc/mem and ptrace-based attacks.

mitigations.name: Restrict File and Directory Permissions
mitigations.detail: Ensure /proc/[pid]/mem is not accessible by unprivileged users via kernel configuration. Modern kernels with YAMA LSM provide ptrace restrictions. Enforce strict AppArmor or SELinux profiles for authentication daemons.

hypotheses.fpr: GDB and strace legitimately use ptrace for debugging — restrict alerts to non-development hosts or when target PID belongs to sshd/sudo/PAM. Developer workstations may trigger /proc/mem access during debugging; allowlist by host role and user account.

hypotheses.title: Core Dump Triggered for Offline Credential Extraction from Linux Process
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on a Linux system is suspected of deliberately triggering a core dump of a credential-holding daemon (sshd, httpd, PAM) to capture process memory for offline credential extraction. Hunt for unusual core dump file creation by authentication-related processes, especially when followed by file collection into an archive or staging directory.

pivots.label: Auditd — gcore or kill SIGSEGV
pivots.detail: Auditd: execve gcore [sshd_pid] by non-root user OR kill -11 [sshd_pid] followed by core dump creation. Also: ulimit -c unlimited set in shell session before a process crash.

pivots.label: Core dump file in staging path
pivots.detail: File creation: core or core.[pid] file in /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp, or current working directory of an attacker-controlled process. Core dumps for sshd are typically 50–200 MB. Unusual size + location + parent process are the key indicators.

pivots.label: strings / grep on core dump
pivots.detail: Process creation: strings core.[pid] OR grep -a 'password\|secret\|key' core.[pid] by a non-developer user immediately after the core dump creation — indicates attacker searching the dump for plaintext credentials.

detection_logic.query_hint: auditd type=CWD AND type=PATH name=*core* AND uid!=0 | followby execve=strings within 120s

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Disable core dumps for sensitive daemons via /etc/security/limits.conf (hard core 0) or systemd LimitCORE=0 in unit files for sshd, httpd, PAM. Core dump handlers (systemd-coredump, apport) should route dumps to a privileged directory.

mitigations.name: Restrict File and Directory Permissions
mitigations.detail: Configure kernel core dump path to a root-only directory (echo '/var/core/core.%e.%p' > /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern). Restrict core dump creation to root by default.

refs.label: Auditd configuration for Linux credential hunting
DFIR Report — Linux core dump credential extraction

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate core dumps occur during application crashes — the key differentiators are: (1) deliberate triggering via gcore or signal, (2) immediate manual inspection of the core dump, (3) non-root user or non-system parent process. Automated crash reporting systems (apport, abrt) create core dumps but do not run strings against them.

hypotheses.title: Direct /etc/shadow Access for Offline Password Hash Extraction
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor with root or backup-level access on a Linux/macOS host is suspected of reading /etc/shadow directly to obtain hashed user passwords for offline cracking. Hunt for non-shadow-management processes (not passwd, useradd, usermod, chage) opening /etc/shadow with read access, particularly when followed by the file being copied to a staging location.

pivots.label: Auditd — /etc/shadow read
pivots.detail: Auditd rule: -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S open,openat -F path=/etc/shadow -F perm=r -k shadow_read. Alert on: comm not in (passwd,useradd,usermod,chage,shadow,chpasswd) AND the opening process is interactive shell (bash, sh, zsh) or a script. Especially alert if auid is not 0 (non-root interactive user with sudo).

pivots.label: Copy or staging of shadow file
pivots.detail: Execve: cp /etc/shadow /tmp/.shadow OR cat /etc/shadow > /tmp/shadow.txt OR python3 -c 'open("/etc/shadow")'. File creation: a new file with shadow-like content (colon-separated, $6$ SHA-512 hash format) in /tmp, /dev/shm, or home directory.

pivots.label: Transfer after staging
pivots.detail: Network: curl, wget, scp, or nc uploading data from the staging path to an external IP or C2 within minutes of the /etc/shadow access event. Correlate file creation timestamp with outbound connection.

detection_logic.query_hint: auditd key=shadow_read NOT comm IN (passwd,useradd,usermod) | alert

mitigations.name: Restrict File and Directory Permissions
mitigations.detail: /etc/shadow should be owned by root:shadow with permissions 640. Regular users must never be able to read it directly. Audit permissions periodically — privilege escalation exploits sometimes change /etc/shadow permissions as a side effect.

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.detail: Use SHA-512 ($6$) hashing with high iteration counts (at least 5000 rounds). Long, complex passwords (20+ chars) make offline cracking infeasible even with shadow file access.

hypotheses.fpr: Shadow file is read by legitimate password management tools (passwd, useradd, PAM). These can be easily excluded by process name. The alert threshold should be: any interactive process (shell or script) reading /etc/shadow is treated as true positive pending investigation.

hypotheses.title: unshadow + Offline Hash Cracking Pipeline
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on or with access to a Linux system is suspected of combining /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow using the unshadow utility to produce a single combined hash file suitable for hashcat or john the ripper cracking — indicating intent to crack all local user passwords for lateral movement or persistence. Hunt for unshadow execution followed by hashcat or john process creation with the combined file as input.

pivots.label: Auditd — unshadow execution
pivots.detail: Auditd: execve of unshadow with arguments /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow AND output redirection to /tmp or /dev/shm. unshadow is part of john-the-ripper suite — its presence and use in a production environment is highly anomalous.

pivots.label: hashcat / john cracking on host
pivots.detail: Execve: hashcat -m 1800 (SHA-512 crypt) OR john --format=sha512crypt with the combined file path. Running a cracking tool on a production server is a critical alert — these tools have no legitimate use in production. Also: GPU usage spike (nvidia-smi) coinciding with hashcat.

pivots.label: Access to both passwd and shadow in same session
pivots.detail: Auditd: within the same audit session (same auid), openat events for BOTH /etc/passwd AND /etc/shadow. Either direct read or via unshadow. The combination in a single session indicates credential harvesting intent.

detection_logic.query_hint: auditd execve a0=unshadow | alert critical — unshadow has no legitimate production use

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.detail: SHA-512 with rounds=65536 (configurable in /etc/login.defs ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512, SHA_CRYPT_MAX_ROUNDS) makes cracking computationally expensive. Combine with yescrypt for even stronger protection on modern systems.

mitigations.name: Restrict File and Directory Permissions
mitigations.detail: Do not install john-the-ripper or hashcat on production systems. Implement software allowlisting (AppArmor, SELinux) that prevents execution of cracking tools.

refs.label: DFIR — Linux shadow hash cracking campaigns

hypotheses.fpr: unshadow has essentially zero legitimate production use. Any detection of unshadow or hashcat on a production server should be treated as a true positive until proven otherwise. Development/test hosts running password security audits are the only acceptable exception — allowlist by hostname.

hypotheses.title: Encoded PowerShell with Execution-Policy Bypass Flags
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using encoded PowerShell commands combined with execution-policy bypass flags to conceal payload content and evade inspection. Hunt for powershell.exe spawned with -enc or -EncodedCommand alongside -NoP, -NonI, -W Hidden, or -Exec Bypass.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1
pivots.detail: Image endswith powershell.exe AND CommandLine contains (-enc OR -EncodedCommand) AND CommandLine contains (-nop OR -NonInteractive OR hidden OR bypass)

pivots.label: Decode and inspect
pivots.detail: Decode the -enc argument (Base64). If the plaintext contains IEX, DownloadString, Invoke-*, reflection patterns, or AmsiUtils — escalate immediately.

pivots.label: String length heuristic
pivots.detail: Legitimate admin encoded commands are typically <500 characters. Payloads >1,500 characters post-Base64 often represent multi-layer compressed or obfuscated payloads.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=1 Image=*powershell.exe CommandLine=*(-enc|-EncodedCommand)* CommandLine=*(-nop|bypass|hidden)*

mitigations.name: Disable or Remove Feature or Program
mitigations.detail: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode via AppLocker or WDAC to block reflection-based attacks. Disable PowerShell v2 (Remove-WindowsFeature MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2).

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Enable Script Block Logging (EID 4104) and Module Logging via GPO. Pair with AMSI integration for runtime payload inspection even when -enc is used.

hypotheses.fpr: SCCM, Intune, and GPO delivery scripts often use encoding for safe transport. Allowlist by signed binary, scheduled task context, execution from C:\Windows\System32 or C:\Program Files, and known admin workstations.

hypotheses.title: In-Memory Download Cradle (Fileless Execution)
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using a PowerShell download cradle — Net.WebClient.DownloadString or Invoke-WebRequest piped into IEX — to fetch and execute a remote payload entirely in memory. Hunt for ScriptBlock log events containing both a web-client download method and an invocation expression within the same or consecutive events.

pivots.label: PS EID 4104 — primary
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (DownloadString OR DownloadData OR WebClient) AND ScriptBlockText contains (IEX OR Invoke-Expression OR &([scriptblock]::Create))

pivots.label: Network correlation
pivots.detail: Correlate EID 4104 match with Sysmon EID 3 from powershell.exe to the same destination within ±5 seconds. Non-browser PS network connections to external IPs or newly-registered domains warrant automatic escalation.

pivots.label: Obfuscated variant
pivots.detail: Attackers split 'DownloadString' across variables or use character arrays. Hunt for Net.WebClient in ScriptBlock text as a stable anchor and flag any block followed within 5 seconds by a second high-entropy ScriptBlock.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=4104 ScriptBlockText=*(DownloadString|DownloadData|WebClient)* ScriptBlockText=*(IEX|Invoke-Expression)*

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict outbound PowerShell access via application proxy — require scripts to route through an authenticated proxy that logs all connections.

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Enable Script Block Logging and enforce Constrained Language Mode. Block Invoke-Expression with downloaded content via AMSI custom rules or EDR behavioral detection.

refs.label: DFIR Report — Cobalt Strike staging chains
Elastic: execution via PowerShell download cradle

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate admin scripts use Invoke-WebRequest to pull resources from known CDNs or internal update servers. Allowlist by destination domain: Microsoft, GitHub, corporate infrastructure. Alert on unknown or new destination domains.

hypotheses.title: AMSI Bypass via PowerShell Reflection
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of patching the AMSI scan interface in memory using .NET reflection to disable antimalware scanning before executing a concealed payload. Hunt for ScriptBlock log events containing AmsiUtils, amsiInitFailed, or reflection-based SetValue calls targeting System.Management.Automation assemblies.

pivots.label: PS EID 4104 — direct
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (AmsiUtils OR amsiInitFailed) OR (ScriptBlockText contains System.Management.Automation AND SetValue AND amsi)

pivots.label: PS EID 4104 — obfuscated
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains [Ref].Assembly.GetType AND System.Management.Automation AND SetValue. Also hunt character-array construction of 'AmsiUtils' via [cHAr] concatenation or -replace/-join patterns.

pivots.label: Behavioral follow-up
pivots.detail: AMSI bypass is almost always followed within seconds by a second ScriptBlock executing the concealed payload. A gap <5 seconds between AmsiUtils ScriptBlock and a high-entropy second block = confirmed evasion chain.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=4104 ScriptBlockText=*(AmsiUtils|amsiInitFailed)* OR ScriptBlockText=*(System.Management.Automation*SetValue*amsi)*

mitigations.name: Antivirus/Antimalware
mitigations.detail: Keep AMSI provider up to date. Deploy EDR with kernel-level ETW monitoring that detects AMSI patching regardless of user-mode hook state.

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode via WDAC — CLM prevents the .NET reflection calls used by most AMSI bypass techniques.

hypotheses.fpr: In production environments outside approved red team windows, legitimate AMSI bypass activity is essentially zero. Alert on any occurrence and investigate promptly.

hypotheses.title: Offensive Framework Cmdlets via ScriptBlock Logging
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of executing PowerShell-based offensive framework modules from PowerSploit, PowerView, Empire, or Mimikatz captured in ScriptBlock logs. Hunt for EID 4104 events containing known offensive cmdlet names across credential dumping, lateral movement, AD enumeration, and defense evasion categories.

pivots.label: Credential dumping
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Invoke-Mimikatz OR Invoke-NinjaCopy OR Get-GPPPassword OR Invoke-Kerberoast OR Invoke-DCSync OR Out-Minidump)

pivots.label: Lateral movement
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Invoke-PsExec OR Invoke-WMICommand OR Invoke-SMBExec OR Invoke-TheHash OR Enter-PSSession)

pivots.label: Discovery & enumeration
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Invoke-BloodHound OR Get-DomainAdmin OR Find-DomainShares OR Invoke-UserHunter OR Get-NetComputer OR Get-NetUser)

pivots.label: Defense evasion
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Set-MpPreference -Disable* OR Remove-MpPreference OR Invoke-BypassUAC OR Invoke-TokenManipulation OR Add-Persistence)

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=4104 ScriptBlockText IN (Invoke-Mimikatz,Invoke-Kerberoast,Invoke-BloodHound,Invoke-DCSync,Get-DomainAdmin,Invoke-PsExec)

mitigations.name: Disable or Remove Feature or Program
mitigations.detail: Remove PowerShell v2 and enforce Constrained Language Mode. PowerView and PowerSploit cmdlets fail under CLM as they require full language mode.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Apply tiered administration to limit Domain Admin rights. Kerberoasting and DCSync are only viable when high-value accounts have exploitable configurations.

refs.label: CISA AA25-141A — Akira PS credential dumping

hypotheses.fpr: The listed cmdlets are exclusively offensive with no legitimate administrative use. FPR is near-zero; any match warrants immediate investigation. EID 4104 requires ScriptBlock logging enabled via GPO.

hypotheses.title: Classic Remote Thread Injection into Legitimate Process
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of injecting malicious code into a legitimate host process using VirtualAllocEx / WriteProcessMemory / CreateRemoteThread to achieve execution under a trusted identity. Hunt for Sysmon EID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) where the source process is unexpected and the target is a common host such as explorer.exe, svchost.exe, or notepad.exe.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 8
pivots.detail: SourceImage NOT IN (known EDR/AV binaries) AND TargetImage IN (explorer.exe, svchost.exe, lsass.exe, notepad.exe, rundll32.exe, dllhost.exe) AND StartAddress NOT startswith TargetImage module base

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 10 correlation
pivots.detail: SourceImage opens handle to TargetImage with GrantedAccess = 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) or 0x43a (PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD + PROCESS_VM_WRITE + PROCESS_VM_OPERATION + PROCESS_VM_READ + QUERY_INFORMATION) within seconds of EID 8.

pivots.label: StartAddress heuristic
pivots.detail: StartAddress in EID 8 pointing to an unbacked memory region (not associated with any loaded module) = shellcode injection. Correlate with Sysmon EID 3 network connection from the target process to a C2 IP within 60 seconds.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=8 SourceImage NOT IN (known EDR/AV) TargetImage IN (explorer.exe,svchost.exe,notepad.exe) | correlate EventCode=3 outbound from TargetImage within 60s

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Deploy EDR with kernel-level process injection detection. Enable Arbitrary Code Guard (ACG) and Code Integrity Guard (CIG) on browser and high-value processes via Windows Exploit Guard.

mitigations.name: Execution Prevention
mitigations.detail: Enable AppLocker or WDAC to prevent unsigned code from running. HVCI prevents unsigned code execution in kernel memory, limiting injector capabilities.

hypotheses.fpr: Some AV/EDR products legitimately inject threads into monitored processes. Allowlist known security product executables by signed binary path. Focus alerting on unsigned or user-space source processes injecting into system processes.

hypotheses.title: Process Hollowing via Suspended Process + Unmapping
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of creating a legitimate process in suspended state, unmapping its memory, and replacing it with malicious code before resuming to masquerade as a trusted binary. Hunt for newly created suspended processes quickly followed by WriteProcessMemory and ResumeThread API calls, especially when the process image does not match the on-disk executable.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 + EID 8
pivots.detail: Process created with CREATE_SUSPENDED flag (no direct Sysmon field — infer from: process created AND immediately followed within 100ms by EID 8 CreateRemoteThread from same parent) targeting known hosts like svchost.exe, notepad.exe, explorer.exe.

pivots.label: Image mismatch (EDR)
pivots.detail: EDR telemetry: ProcessImage (from PE header in memory) does not match ProcessPath (on-disk path). This is the definitive indicator of hollow process — requires EDR with memory scanning capability.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 3 anomaly
pivots.detail: svchost.exe or notepad.exe initiating outbound TCP connections to non-Microsoft IPs on unusual ports (4444, 8080, 443 with non-browser UA) is a strong behavioral indicator of a hollowed process executing C2 traffic.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=8 TargetImage IN (svchost.exe,notepad.exe,explorer.exe) | correlate EventCode=3 outbound from same TargetImage within 60s

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Enable EDR memory scanning to detect PE headers in non-module-backed memory regions. Arbitrary Code Guard (ACG) prevents dynamic code patching in protected processes.

mitigations.name: Execution Prevention
mitigations.detail: WDAC with HVCI blocks most process hollowing by preventing unsigned code from executing — the injected PE cannot meet code integrity requirements.

hypotheses.fpr: Application installers and legitimate virtualization software occasionally create suspended processes. Alert only when combined with unusual network behavior from the target process or a parent-child relationship mismatch.

hypotheses.title: DLL Injection via LoadLibrary or Reflective DLL
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of injecting a malicious DLL into a running process by writing its path to remote memory and calling LoadLibraryA/W via CreateRemoteThread, or loading a PE directly from memory via reflective loading. Hunt for Sysmon EID 7 (ImageLoaded) events where a DLL is loaded from a user-writable or temp path into a system process.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 7
pivots.detail: ImageLoaded path matches (%TEMP%\* OR %APPDATA%\* OR C:\Users\*\Downloads\* OR C:\ProgramData\*) AND Image IN (explorer.exe, svchost.exe, notepad.exe, rundll32.exe) AND Signed = false

pivots.label: Reflective DLL marker
pivots.detail: Reflective DLLs load without touching disk — detectable via EDR memory scanning for PE headers in non-module-backed memory regions. Hunt processes with no corresponding ImageLoaded event for memory regions executing code.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 8 + EID 7 chain
pivots.detail: EID 8 CreateRemoteThread into target process within 2 seconds of EID 7 showing unsigned DLL loaded into that same target process = high-confidence injection chain.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=7 Image IN (svchost.exe,explorer.exe,notepad.exe) ImageLoaded path IN (%TEMP%,%APPDATA%,C:\Users\*\Downloads) Signed=false

mitigations.name: Execution Prevention
mitigations.detail: Enable WDAC or AppLocker to prevent unsigned DLLs from loading in system processes. HVCI enforces DLL code integrity at the kernel level.

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Enable Sysmon EID 7 with filters for unsigned or temp-path DLLs in system processes. EDR behavioral rules detecting LoadLibrary calls to user-writable paths.

refs.label: CISA AA23-193A — Advanced Persistent Threat TTPs

hypotheses.fpr: Some legitimate software loads DLLs from AppData (e.g., browser extensions, plugin frameworks). Focus on system processes loading unsigned DLLs from user-writable paths — this combination has very low FPR.

hypotheses.title: Valid Account Logon from Anomalous Source
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor is suspected of authenticating with a legitimate stolen or compromised credential from an unusual source IP, geography, or at an abnormal time to blend in with normal operations. Hunt for successful logon events (EID 4624) for privileged or service accounts from IPs not in the expected baseline, especially outside business hours or from cloud/VPN exit nodes.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4624
pivots.detail: LogonType IN (2, 3, 10) AND TargetUserName NOT endswith $ AND IpAddress NOT IN (known_office_ranges, VPN_ranges) AND TargetUserName IN (admin accounts, service accounts, IT staff). Time window: 20:00–06:00 local = elevated priority.

pivots.label: Impossible travel
pivots.detail: Same account (TargetUserName) with successful 4624 from two geographically distant IPs within a time window that makes travel physically impossible. Requires GeoIP enrichment on IpAddress field.

pivots.label: New account first use
pivots.detail: TargetUserName last seen >30 days ago suddenly authenticating. Compare 4624 against account last-logon baseline in Active Directory. Reactivated dormant accounts are a strong persistence indicator.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=4624 LogonType IN (2,3,10) IpAddress NOT IN (known_ranges) TargetUserName NOT endswith $ | enrich with GeoIP for impossible travel

mitigations.name: Multi-factor Authentication
mitigations.detail: Enforce MFA for all privileged and remote access. Compromised credentials alone are insufficient when MFA is required — especially for VPN, RDP, and cloud console access.

mitigations.name: Account Use Policies
mitigations.detail: Implement sign-in risk policies with conditional access — block or challenge logons from IPs with no prior history for the account, especially outside business hours.

refs.label: CISA AA24-038A — Volt Typhoon valid accounts

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate remote work, travel, and VPN use generate off-baseline logons. Build a per-account IP/geo/time baseline over 30 days before alerting. Service accounts should never log on interactively — apply stricter thresholds.

hypotheses.title: Service Account Interactive or Network Logon
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor with knowledge of a service account credential is suspected of using it interactively or over the network to move laterally, bypassing human-account monitoring. Hunt for service accounts (accounts with names matching service naming conventions) logging on with LogonType 2 (interactive) or 10 (remote interactive) which are inconsistent with normal service account usage.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4624
pivots.detail: TargetUserName matches (svc_*, *_svc, *service*, *sa_*, *sql*, *iis*, *exchange*) AND LogonType IN (2, 10) — service accounts should only produce LogonType 5 (service). Any interactive logon is anomalous.

pivots.label: 4624 LogonType 3 from unexpected host
pivots.detail: Service account authenticating via network logon (Type 3) from a workstation rather than its designated server. TargetUserName = service account AND WorkstationName NOT IN (expected server list).

pivots.label: 4648 Explicit credential use
pivots.detail: WinEvt 4648 (logon with explicit credentials) where SubjectUserName != TargetUserName and TargetUserName is a service account indicates credential stuffing or pass-the-password of a service credential.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=4624 LogonType IN (2,10) TargetUserName IN (*svc*,*sa_*,*sql*,*iis*,*exchange*) | alert critical

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Implement Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) — passwords are 240-bit random and automatically rotated, making them unusable for interactive logons even if extracted.

mitigations.name: Account Use Policies
mitigations.detail: Apply User Rights Assignment GPO: Deny log on locally and Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services for all service accounts. Service accounts should only authenticate via LogonType 5 (service).

hypotheses.fpr: Some managed service accounts (gMSA) and scheduled tasks produce Type 3 logons from servers. Document expected service account logon patterns per account — alert on any deviation from the documented baseline.

hypotheses.title: RDP Lateral Movement from Non-Admin Workstation
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using RDP to move laterally from a compromised workstation to servers or other workstations, leveraging stolen credentials to expand access. Hunt for EID 4624 LogonType 10 (RemoteInteractive) originating from workstation-class source IPs combined with mstsc.exe process creation on the same source host.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4624 on destination
pivots.detail: LogonType = 10 AND IpAddress matches workstation subnet (not server subnet, not IT admin jump hosts) AND TargetUserName not in (expected RDP users list). Workstation-to-workstation RDP is almost never legitimate.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 on source
pivots.detail: Image = mstsc.exe (RDP client) launched from cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or a non-desktop shortcut parent. mstsc.exe with command-line arguments (/v:target /admin) indicates automated lateral movement.

pivots.label: EID 4778 / 4779
pivots.detail: WinEvt 4778 (session reconnect) or 4779 (session disconnect) from unusual IPs immediately before 4624 Type 10 indicates adversary cycling through RDP sessions across multiple hosts.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=4624 LogonType=10 IpAddress IN (workstation_subnets) TargetUserName NOT IN (admin_rdp_users) | alert high

mitigations.name: Limit Access to Resource Over Network
mitigations.detail: Restrict RDP access to only designated jump hosts via host-based firewall rules. Block TCP 3389 between workstations at the network level.

mitigations.name: Multi-factor Authentication
mitigations.detail: Require MFA for all RDP sessions via NLA + MFA. Compromised credentials alone cannot initiate RDP when MFA is enforced at the gateway or host level.

refs.label: CISA AA23-075A — LockBit RDP lateral movement

hypotheses.fpr: IT helpdesk and server administrators legitimately use RDP. Allowlist by source IP (jump hosts, IT subnet) and time window (business hours). Alert on workstation-to-workstation RDP and after-hours sessions from non-IT accounts.

hypotheses.title: RDP Enabled on Previously Unexposed Host
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of enabling RDP on a host where it was previously disabled or blocked, creating a persistent remote access channel. Hunt for registry modifications enabling RDP (fDenyTSConnections = 0), firewall rule additions for port 3389, or the first-ever EID 4624 LogonType 10 on a host with no prior RDP history.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 registry
pivots.detail: TargetObject = HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\fDenyTSConnections AND Details = DWORD:0 — this key being set to 0 enables RDP. Alert immediately on any modification.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4688 — netsh firewall
pivots.detail: CommandLine contains (netsh advfirewall firewall add rule) AND CommandLine contains (3389 OR RDP OR RemoteDesktop) — adversaries commonly open 3389 via netsh before enabling RDP via registry.

pivots.label: First RDP logon baseline
pivots.detail: Host with no EID 4624 LogonType 10 events in the prior 30 days suddenly receiving a Type 10 logon. Baseline per-host RDP logon history and alert on first occurrence outside a change-management window.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=13 TargetObject=*fDenyTSConnections Details=DWORD:0 | alert and investigate immediately

mitigations.name: Operating System Configuration
mitigations.detail: Enforce fDenyTSConnections=1 via GPO to keep RDP disabled by default. Prevent registry key modification via SACL auditing and EDR registry protection rules.

mitigations.name: Network Segmentation
mitigations.detail: Block TCP 3389 from non-management VLANs at the network perimeter. Even if RDP is enabled on a host, network segmentation prevents adversary connectivity.

refs.label: CISA AA24-038A — Volt Typhoon RDP enabling

hypotheses.fpr: IT administrators legitimately enable RDP during provisioning. Allowlist changes originating from IT management tools (SCCM, Ansible, DSC). Alert on manual registry edits by interactive user sessions outside change windows.

hypotheses.title: WMI Used to Spawn Process for Lateral Movement or Execution
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using Windows Management Instrumentation to remotely execute commands or spawn processes on target hosts, bypassing standard remote execution controls. Hunt for processes with a WMI provider host parent (WmiPrvSE.exe) launching shells, scripting engines, or LOLBINs.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — WMI child
pivots.detail: ParentImage endswith WmiPrvSE.exe AND Image IN (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, cscript.exe, wscript.exe, mshta.exe, certutil.exe, bitsadmin.exe, rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe)

pivots.label: WinEvt 4688 — WMI child process
pivots.detail: NewProcessName matches (cmd.exe, powershell.exe) AND ParentProcessName = C:\Windows\System32\wbem\WmiPrvSE.exe. WmiPrvSE spawning shells is almost never legitimate in production.

pivots.label: Network WMI (DCOM)
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 3: DestinationPort = 135 (DCOM endpoint mapper) followed within 10 seconds by EID 1 with WmiPrvSE.exe parent on the target host. Source host is a lateral movement pivot point.

detection_logic.query_hint: EventCode=1 ParentImage=*WmiPrvSE.exe Image IN (cmd.exe,powershell.exe,cscript.exe,wscript.exe,mshta.exe,rundll32.exe)

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict which accounts can invoke WMI remotely via DCOM permissions. Limit WMI namespace access via WMI Access Control on root\cimv2.

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.detail: Block WmiPrvSE.exe from spawning interactive shells via WDAC child process rules. Enable WMI activity logging (Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational) for monitoring.

hypotheses.fpr: SCCM, monitoring agents, and some backup solutions use WMI for legitimate management. Allowlist WmiPrvSE.exe child processes spawned under SYSTEM in the context of known management server IPs. Alert on interactive or network-sourced WMI execution.

hypotheses.title: WMI Subscription for Persistence
